summary: Root cause (confidence 0.72, medium): ledger-db's filesystem filled to 100% because the inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' retained WAL (~34GB→77GB at ~2.4–2.9 GB/min), and once WAL/temp and relation files could no longer be extended every writer to the shared ledger-db began failing with 'No space left on device'. This began before the payment-service v6.0.0 deploy (disk was already 89% at 13:00Z and 98.6% at 14:45Z) and did not inflect at 14:46Z, and it never recovered after the 15:12Z rollback (disk pinned at 100%, extend errors continuing to 16:56:40Z), which rules out the writer-code/rollback hypotheses. payment-service v6.0.0 (MANDATE_HOLD / new entry type) is not the origin: its error string, its flat pool/latency profile, and a second writer (order-service) emitting the identical storage error at the same onset all point to the datastore. Immediate fix is on the ledger-db side — reclaim WAL/disk (drop or re-activate the inactive analytics_cdc slot), not further payment-service changes.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Independent ledger-db disk/WAL exhaustion: inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' retains WAL until disk full (resource_exhaustion)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' on the shared ledger-db retained WAL (growing ~34GB->77GB, ~2.4-2.9 GB/min) driving disk from 89% (13:00Z) to 100% (15:00Z) independent of any deploy. When WAL/temp and relation files could no longer be extended, ledger-db emitted 'No space left on device' and EVERY writer failed. Fault originates in ledger-db storage exhaustion, not in payment-service.

causal_chain.claim: Inactive replication slot analytics_cdc retains WAL on ledger-db
Retained WAL grows ~34GB->77GB (~2.4-2.9 GB/min), driving disk_used_pct 89%->100% monotonically from 13:00Z, well before the 14:46Z deploy
ledger-db warns at 98% then errors/panics writing pg_wal/xlogtemp and cannot extend base/... files
Disk exhaustion propagates to every shared ledger-db writer, not just the changed one
payment-service, order-service and settlement-service all surface storage-style failures / ~50-60% error rates at the same 14:56-15:00Z onset
Rollback of the writer does not free disk, so failures persist past 15:12Z

assumptions: The analytics_cdc slot (not write volume) is the dominant driver of the retained-WAL growth; no tool exposes pg_replication_slots to confirm origin/age
settlement-service's ~55% metric spike is the same storage signature (its logs show zero ERROR/WARN, so verbatim confirmation is missing)

ranked_hypotheses.title: v6.0.0 mandate flow accelerated ledger write/WAL volume, tipping an already-near-full disk (bad_deployment as trigger of a resource failure)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: payment-service v6.0.0's new mandate flow increased ledger write/WAL volume, advancing the disk-exhaustion threshold and causing the storage error. Fault originates in the release.

causal_chain.claim: payment-service v6.0.0 (14:46Z) introduces mandate create/approve endpoints writing MANDATE_HOLD
New flow raises ledger write/WAL generation rate above prior baseline
ledger-db disk (already 89-98%) reaches 100% faster
Writers fail on storage; payment-service error rate jumps to 60%

assumptions: Write volume from the mandate flow measurably increased WAL/disk growth rate (contradicted by F35/F36 - growth rate is unchanged-or-lower post-deploy)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Rollback is a red herring: retry storm / queue saturation, not entry-type rejection
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Error rate driven by retry storms or queue saturation from the new flow, not by rejected entry type; failures would persist or decay slowly after rollback.

causal_chain.claim: New mandate flow produces retries/queue pressure
Retry amplification or kafka queue saturation drives sustained error rate
Failure persists after rollback

assumptions: a retry/queue mechanism exists independent of the entry type
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F16/F28 show 100% of errors are a single storage-exhaustion pattern (no timeout/pool/deadlock signatures); F20 shows flat db_pool_in_use and flat p99 latency. While post-rollback persistence (F32) is real, it is fully explained by H2 (disk stays full); no retry/queue signature is present.

ranked_hypotheses.title: payment-service-specific resource/downstream failure confined to the changed writer
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The storage error string in payment-service may originate from a resource or downstream failure specific to payment-service's write path (its own local/temp filesystem, connection to ledger-db, or bank-partner-api/kafka path) rather than from ledger-db's own disk.

causal_chain.claim: payment-service v6.0.0 write path fails on 'No space left on device'
The 'No space' condition is local to payment-service or its immediate dependency, not ledger-db
Other ledger-db writers would be unaffected

assumptions: payment-service could host or proxy a filesystem that fills independently
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F18 shows the 'No space left on device'/xlogtemp failure originates inside ledger-db, and F27/F28/F29 show order-service and settlement-service failing at the same onset with order-service emitting the identical storage string. A payment-service-local filesystem failure cannot explain simultaneous failures in three independent writers. F31 is odd but insufficient to localize the fault to payment-service.

ranked_hypotheses.title: MANDATE_HOLD write triggers ledger-db validation/enum contract break (reporter's assumption)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The new mandate flow writes MANDATE_HOLD into ledger-db; the schema/enum rejects it, producing ledger write failures. Fault originates in the writer's contract change.

causal_chain.claim: v6.0.0 introduces MANDATE_HOLD ledger entry type
ledger-db schema/enum rejects the unknown entry type
ledger write failures and 60% error rate

assumptions: ledger-db enforces an enum whitelist MANDATE_HOLD violates
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F16/F28: 100% of errors in two independent services are 'No space left on device', a storage error, not a validation/enum rejection. F18 confirms inbound DB storage exhaustion. F27/F29 show THREE writers failing simultaneously. No type-rejection signature exists anywhere.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared kafka broker / producer-consumer contract failure (queue path)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: v6.0.0's new flow emits changed messages to the shared kafka broker used by order-service and consumed by settlement-service/notification-service; a producer/consumer contract or broker saturation drives multi-service error spikes at the same onset.

causal_chain.claim: v6.0.0 produces messages to shared kafka
Shared broker/consumer contract issue propagates to payment/order/settlement
Multi-service error spike at ~15:00Z

assumptions: kafka failures would emit 'No space left on device' error strings in payment-service (unlikely)
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F16/F28 error strings are DB storage errors ('No space left on device', 'FAILED INSERT'), not kafka produce/consume errors; F18 attributes the failure to ledger-db filesystem; settlement-service shows no queue-consumer log signature (F30). Kafka is not the origin of the observed failure signature.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Version skew / incomplete rollout across the shared journal-entry contract
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Part of the fleet or a dependent service was upgraded so v6.0.0 writers hit old readers. Requires multiple deployments or a partial-rollout record.

causal_chain.claim: v6.0.0 writers emit new contract while others remain old
Writers hit old readers and writes fail
Skew persists until all services upgraded

assumptions: multiple deployments or a partial fleet rollout exist
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F7/F8: exactly one deployment across all services in the window. F4/F2/F22/F23: no ledger-db or config change. F16/F28: failure signature is storage, not a reader contract mismatch.

facts.statement: ledger-db is a shared postgres datastore written by four services (order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service, settlement-service); the failure is datastore-wide, not confined to the changed writer.

ledger-db disk_used_pct rose monotonically from 89.18% at 13:00Z to 98.62% at 14:45Z, 99.8% at 14:52Z, and pinned at 100.0% from the 15:00Z bucket onward — the storage trend predates and is independent of the 14:46Z deploy.
The disk growth rate did not inflect at the 14:46Z deploy: ~9.3 pp/30 min before the deploy, ~6.8 pp/30 min after (bounded by reaching 100%).
WAL retained by the inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' grew ~33.9 GB → ~77.4 GB at ~2.4–2.9 GB/min with no larger rate after the deploy (~2.86 GB/min pre-deploy vs ~2.42 GB/min post-deploy).

ledger-db itself emitted the storage-exhaustion errors: WARN 'disk usage 98% on /var/lib/postgresql/data' at 14:48:20Z, then ERROR/PANIC 'could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.<n>": No space left on device' (first 15:01:01Z) and 'could not extend file "base/16402/2619"' (first 15:01:39Z).
100% of payment-service's matched ERRORs (59) are a single pattern: 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device'; earliest at 15:00:26Z.

order-service, a second shared ledger-db writer, emitted the identical storage string ('INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device', 236 errors, first 15:00:42Z) and spiked to ~48–50% error rate at the same onset.

settlement-service, a third shared ledger-db writer, showed an independent error-rate spike at the same onset (0.15% in the 14:50Z bucket → 18.01% avg at 14:56Z, sustained ~54–56% to 16:56Z) with zero ERROR/WARN log lines available in the log store.
payment-service shows no resource anomaly of its own: db_pool_in_use flat (~7.75–8.31 connections) and latency_p99_ms flat (~312–337 ms) before and during the error spike.

ledger-db write-volume-related metrics show no step at 14:46Z: connections_active flat ~60.5–62.7, cpu_pct flat ~28.6–31.0, slow_queries_per_min flat ~0.6–1.3, and replication_lag_ms rising gently and monotonically from ~3101 ms (14:20Z) to ~3881 ms (15:08Z).
payment-service did NOT recover after the 15:12Z rollback: error_rate stayed ~55–70% in every bucket from 15:10Z through the final 16:55Z bucket.

The disk-full condition was unresolved at end of data: ledger-db disk_used_pct was exactly 100.0% in every bucket from 15:00Z to 16:57Z, and the base/16402/2619 extend errors continued to 16:56:40Z (~1h44m past rollback).

Exactly one deployment existed across all services in the incident window and the full prior week: payment-service v6.0.0 (dep-6203, 'New UPI mandate flow', new entry type MANDATE_HOLD), deployed 14:46Z, rolled back 15:12Z; no ledger-db/schema/migration deployment exists.

The change/config tool recorded zero config, flag, schema-migration or replication-slot changes across all services over the full 30-day pre-incident window, and zero ledger-db config/deploy changes over a month.

HIST-114 (2025-04-18) is a near-exact precedent (match_score 7): ledger-db 'disk full from retained WAL', symptoms 'no space left on device'/'write failures', root cause 'Inactive replication slot retained WAL until disk filled', resolution 'Dropped slot; added slot-lag alert'.
portfolio-service, a fourth shared ledger-db writer, was completely unaffected (error_rate ~0.15–0.25%, no onset, zero matched ERROR logs) despite the disk being full.

All 139 extend-failures target one single relation (base/16402/2619) while connections stay flat, so writers whose tables were already allocated are not blocked by the full disk — consistent with one writer remaining unaffected.

No named owner/consumer is discoverable for the analytics_cdc slot: no analytics/CDC consumer appears in ledger-db's dependency graph, and 30-day change history shows 0 config changes and 1 unrelated deployment.
No historical incident matches a 'new ledger entry type / MANDATE_HOLD / schema-enum' ledger-db failure; the closest schema/deploy precedent (HIST-111) is a missing-index query issue.

assumptions: The analytics_cdc replication slot — rather than mandate-flow write volume — is the dominant driver of the retained-WAL growth; no tool exposes pg_replication_slots to confirm the slot's origin, age or liveness.

The analytics_cdc slot was already inactive and long-lived before the incident window (only 'retaining <n> MB of WAL' log lines exist; the change-history tools expose no slot creation/drop artifact type), so its disk fill-up is not attributable to a change in the window.

settlement-service's ~55% metric spike reflects the same ledger-db storage exhaustion as the other writers; its log store contains no ERROR/WARN string to confirm this verbatim (log-store blind spot).

order-service and settlement-service write to ledger-db tables that were already allocated or write paths that hit the same storage limit; the exact per-writer blocking differs due to relation-level file extension, not a different root cause.
The relation base/16402/2619 belongs to a table that one of the ledger-db writers (not portfolio-service) writes; log data never names its table/schema owner.

Any lease/ownership of the analytics_cdc slot by an analytics/CDC pipeline cannot be resolved from available change artifacts; the absence of a named owner may be a tool coverage limit rather than proof no owner exists.

The 100% disk occupancy at end of data means no remediation (slot drop, WAL archive/free, restart) had taken effect by 16:59Z; this is inferred from the absence of any recovery signal beyond disk/extend-error continuity.

recommended_actions.action: On ledger-db: free the disk — stop the WAL retention by resolving the inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' (drop it if unused, or re-activate/repair its consumer), then archive/remove reclaimable WAL and verify disk_used_pct falls below 100%. Treat as the primary mitigation; do not make further payment-service changes.
recommended_actions.rationale: Root cause is ledger-db storage exhaustion from WAL retained by the inactive analytics_cdc slot; disk pinned at 100% and extend errors were still occurring 1h44m after the rollback, so writer-side changes cannot clear it. HIST-114 (same mechanism, match_score 7) was resolved exactly this way ('Dropped slot; added slot-lag alert').

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll payment-service forward again or treat v6.0.0/MANDATE_HOLD as the cause pending disk recovery; keep dep-6203 in its rolled-back state and note in the incident channel that the rollback did not mitigate.
recommended_actions.rationale: H3/H1's writer-code mechanism is contradicted: disk slope and WAL rate were unchanged across the 14:46Z deploy, and the 15:12Z rollback produced no recovery while disk stayed at 100%.

recommended_actions.action: Confirm blast radius and recovery: verify ledger-db disk_used_pct returns below 100% and that order-service and settlement-service error rates (spikes at 14:56Z) return to baseline alongside payment-service.
recommended_actions.rationale: The fault is datastore-wide; recovery must be observed on all three affected shared writers, not just payment-service.

recommended_actions.action: Add a replication-slot lag/retention monitor and alert on ledger-db (inactive slot → WAL bytes retained → disk_used_pct threshold), and expose pg_wal_size / replication-slot age metrics, which ledger-db currently lacks (its metric set is only connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min).
recommended_actions.rationale: The failure was only observable indirectly via disk_used_pct and two sparse 'retaining <n> MB of WAL' WARN lines; a slot-lag alert is the recorded fix for the HIST-114 precedent and would have caught the 34→77 GB ramp before 100%.

recommended_actions.action: Identify and fix the owner/consumer of the analytics_cdc slot (find the analytics/CDC pipeline that stopped consuming) and add a lifecycle gate so CDC slots cannot be left inactive indefinitely.
recommended_actions.rationale: The slot is the retention mechanism but its owner/liveness is unresolved — no analytics/CDC node appears in ledger-db's dependency graph or 30-day change history, so the retention can recur.

recommended_actions.action: Add disk-capacity and WAL-retention alerts on the shared ledger-db with capacity headroom, and review shared-datastore write paths for per-relation allocation failure modes (writers hit 'could not extend file base/16402/2619' while other writers kept working).
recommended_actions.rationale: The disk trend was visible ~2.75 hours before the outage (89% at 13:00Z) with no alert; per-relation blocking explains why only some of the four writers failed.

data_gaps: No tool exposes pg_replication_slots (or raw DDL/migration files), so the analytics_cdc slot's creation time, age, last-consumed position and owner could not be verified — the slot's liveness/ownership is inferred from log lines plus the HIST-114 precedent only.

ledger-db has no WAL-size, xlog-bytes, write/transaction-throughput or IOPS metric; WAL growth could only be estimated from 3 sparse 'retaining <n> MB of WAL' WARN lines (14:34:05Z, 14:46:32Z, 14:49:47Z) and disk_used_pct with 3–4 min buckets, so a small (<10%) mandate-driven write increase hidden inside a bucket cannot be fully excluded.

settlement-service's ~55% error spike has no matching log signature: its logs in 14:50–16:59Z contain zero ERROR/WARN (only benign INFO, confirmed continuous to 16:55:36Z, missing_points 0), and the targeted 'space'/'extend' log queries returned 0 — so its spike could not be verbatim-confirmed as the same storage signature.

settlement-service's resource metrics (db_pool_in_use, consumer_lag, latency_p99, cpu_pct) were not retrieved (tool budget exhausted), so its profile could not be compared against payment-service's flat profile.
No catalog/ownership mapping for relation base/16402/2619 was retrievable, so which writer's table is blocked remains undetermined from ledger-db logs.

No per-writer metric (e.g. connections/write counters per client) exists on ledger-db, so it could not be numerically shown that portfolio-service kept writing while others failed — only the absence of any portfolio-related log line and the absence of per-client metrics.

Config-change tool returns 0 for all services across 30 days and no schema-migration artifact type exists, so a ledger-db schema/enum migration accompanying MANDATE_HOLD is neither confirmed nor refuted by an artifact (it is only ruled out as a captured deploy/config change).

No post-rollback remediation signal (slot drop/restart/cleanup) could be checked; only disk_used_pct=100% and continuing extend errors to 16:56:40Z were observed, indicating no effective remediation within the window.
payment-service deploy/config history beyond the single dep-6203 record could not be enumerated (budget exhausted), and no per-instance breakdown of its error rate was obtained.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Finding that the analytics_cdc replication slot is active/healthy (or was newly created within 2026-05-25..2026-06-01), which would move causation toward a change/incomplete-CDC-consumer setup rather than long-term inaction — and would shift blame toward the CDC pipeline owner.

A measured material increase in ledger-db WAL/write/transaction throughput (or mandate-flow write volume) immediately after 14:46Z that is not explained by the slot — i.e. a real inflection in the growth rate — which would revive H3 (v6.0.0 write amplification as the trigger).

Evidence that payment-service-specific writes (MANDATE_HOLD, own temp filesystem, or downstream bank-partner-api/kafka path) were the only blocked writes, contradicting the order-service and settlement-service same-onset failures — which would revive H6.
Any schema/enum rejection or validation error for MANDATE_HOLD in ledger-db logs or DDL, which would revive H1 despite 100% storage-signature errors elsewhere.

Recovery of payment-service (and peers) at 15:12Z after the rollback once disk data is inspected at finer granularity, or restart of ledger-db alone clearing all three writers, which would change the mitigation ordering.

Verbatim confirmation that settlement-service's ~55% spike carries a different (non-storage, e.g. kafka-consumer) signature, which would require splitting the incident into a second, distinct failure mode.

Widening the config-change search to all services across 2026-05-25T00:00Z-2026-06-01T17:00Z (the full pre-incident week) returns count 0: no config, flag, schema-migration or replication-slot configuration change was captured by the config tool anywhere in that window.
Service-scoped queries confirm zero ledger-db deployments and zero ledger-db config changes over 2026-05-01T00:00Z-2026-06-01T17:00Z, i.e. a month-wide window, not just the incident week.

The full-week deployment query across all services (2026-05-25 to 2026-06-01T17:00Z) returns exactly one deployment, dep-6203 (payment-service v6.0.0, 'new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD', rolled_back at 2026-06-01T15:12:00Z); no ledger-db/schema/migration deploy exists in the whole pre-incident week.

ledger-db is a shared postgres datastore (owner platform) written by order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service (all kind db); no analytics/CDC consumer service appears in ledger-db's dependency graph at depth 2 — only the four writer services plus api-gateway callers are listed.

findings.statement: order-service, a second shared ledger-db writer, spikes to a ~48-50% error_rate at the same onset as payment-service: flat 0.22% (max 0.29) in the 14:50Z bucket, then 16.1% avg (max 49.57) in the 14:56Z bucket, and sustained ~47-49% through 16:56Z (last avg 47.54). This is the same onset shape as payment-service and shows the fault is datastore-wide, not confined to the changed writer.

order-service emits the SAME verbatim storage-exhaustion string as payment-service: 236 ERRORs, ALL one pattern 'INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device', first at 2026-06-01T15:00:42Z (last 16:57:47Z). This confirms the shared ledger-db disk exhaustion propagates beyond payment-service.

findings.statement: settlement-service (also a shared ledger-db writer) shows an independent error_rate spike at the same onset: 0.15% in the 14:50Z bucket, then 18.01% avg (max 54.52) at 14:56Z, sustained ~54-56% through 16:56Z (last avg 55.28). This is a THIRD service with the same-timed spike.

settlement-service has NO ERROR or WARN logs at all in 14:50-16:59Z: query for min_level ERROR returned total_matched 0 (data_range 11:00Z-16:59Z, truncated false), and min_level WARN also returned total_matched 0. So its ~55% error spike is visible in metrics but carries no matching application log signature in the log store.

portfolio-service, a fourth shared ledger-db writer, is COMPLETELY UNAFFECTED: error_rate stays ~0.15-0.25% (max 0.32) across every bucket from 14:50Z through 16:56Z, with no onset at all (summary mean 0.21, max 0.32, missing_points 0). It does NOT show the 'No space left on device' signature; its ERROR-log query also returned total_matched 0.

payment-service did NOT recover after the 15:12Z rollback: error_rate remains elevated at ~55-70% (mean 62.29, max 70.45) in every 5-minute bucket from 15:10Z through the final 16:55Z bucket (last avg 63.76), continuing ~1h47m past the rollback. This contradicts the writer-code/rollback hypothesis (H1/H3).

ledger-db exposes only 5 metrics: connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min. There is NO pg_wal_size, xlog, WAL-bytes, write-throughput, transaction-rate or IOPS metric on this component, so WAL/IOPS growth can only be measured via disk_used_pct and the 'retaining <n> MB of WAL' log line.

BEFORE the 14:46Z deploy, disk_used_pct rises monotonically from 89.3% at 13:00Z to 98.62% at 14:45Z (mean 93.93) — i.e. the slope is ~9.3 percentage points per 30 min, the same slope as after 14:46Z. The storage trend is already ~9-10 pp/hour steeper than a '15 minutes after release' onset would allow.

AFTER the deploy (14:45Z-15:00Z), disk_used_pct continues along the same trajectory: 98.65 -> 99.26 -> 99.29 -> 99.80 -> 99.97 -> 100.0, i.e. ~1.35 pp over 12 min (~6.8 pp/30 min, slightly SLOWER than the pre-deploy slope, bounded only by hitting 100%). Rate is unchanged-or-lower; there is no inflection at 14:46Z.

WAL retained by the inactive slot 'analytics_cdc' grows at ~2.4 GB/min BOTH before and after the deploy: 33916 MB at 14:34:05Z -> 69518 MB at 14:46:32Z is lotionw#35599 MB in 12.45 min ≈ 2.86 GB/min (the 14:46:32Z sample is ~30 s AFTER the 14:46Z deploy, so the big pre-deploy step is pre-deploy growth); 69518 -> 77371 MB from 14:46:32Z to 14:49:47Z is 7853 MB in 3.25 min ≈ 2.42 GB/min. The post-deploy WAL rate is no larger than the pre-deploy rate.

No ledger-db write-volume/transaction, connection-count, CPU or slow-query metric steps up at 14:46Z: connections_active is flat ~60.5-62.7 (max 66.7) from 14:20Z through 15:08Z; cpu_pct flat ~28.6-31.0 (max 32.8) across 14:20-15:08Z; slow_queries_per_min flat ~0.6-1.3 (max 1.75) with the highest value at 15:08Z, well after the deploy. No step change at 14:44Z->14:48Z in any of them.

ledger-db replication_lag_ms rises gradually and monotonically from ~3101 ms at 14:20Z to ~3881 ms at 15:08Z, with no discontinuity at the 14:46Z deploy (14:44Z avg 3487.77, 14:48Z avg 3659.38 — same gentle upward drift that was already present from 14:20Z). The lag is a pre-existing, deploy-independent trend consistent with the inactive replication slot, not a post-deploy step.

settlement-service metric ingestion shows NO gap in this window: error_rate has missing_points 0 across 130 total points (summary min 0.1, max 58.62, mean 50.71), and request_rate likewise has missing_points 0 (total_points 130, mean 63.43) with no drop during the outage (14:50Z avg 61.78 -> 16:56Z avg 64.39), so the service kept receiving/serving the same request volume while erroring.

settlement-service's own error_rate in its 14:50Z bucket is healthy (avg 0.15, max 0.22) and the 14:56Z bucket is the first with an elevated average (avg 18.01, max 54.52), consistent with the shared onset in the other ledger writers; its db_pool_in_use and consumer_lag could not be retrieved because the tool budget was exhausted.

Over the full 30-day pre-incident window (2026-05-02T00:00Z to 2026-06-01T17:00Z), the config-change tool reports count 0 across ALL services: no creation, reconfiguration, flag, schema-migration or replication-slot change of any service (thus no recorded analytics_cdc CDC-pipeline/slot change) exists in the 30 days before the incident.

The same 30-day window returns exactly ONE deployment artifact across all services: dep-6203, payment-service v6.0.0, deployed 2026-06-01T14:46:00Z by p.nair, summary 'New UPI mandate flow', rolled_back at 2026-06-01T15:12:00Z. There is NO deployment artifact for an analytics_cdc CDC pipeline, any other consumer group, ledger-db, or a schema/slot change anywhere in the 30 days.

The only historical artifact naming the slot mechanism resolves to HIST-114 (2025-04-18), whose root cause is 'Inactive replication slot retained WAL until disk filled' and whose resolution is 'Dropped slot; added slot-lag alert'. This is the sole precedent tying a replication slot to ledger-db disk exhaustion; the search returned no incident naming the 'analytics_cdc' slot, a CDC consumer service, or a slot owner.

findings.statement: Change-history evidence provides NO named owner/consumer service for the 'analytics_cdc' slot: 30 days of config changes (all services) = 0 hits and 30 days of deployments (all services) = 1 hit (dep-6203, unrelated to CDC). Combined with the previously established absence of any analytics/CDC consumer node in ledger-db's dependency graph (F24), the change-history record cannot name who owns or consumes the slot.

ledger-db disk_used_pct is pinned at exactly 100.0% in every 3-minute bucket from 2026-06-01T15:00:00Z through 2026-06-01T16:57:00Z: summary min=100, max=100, mean=100.0, missing_points=0, total_points=120. It never dropped below 100% at or after the 15:12Z rollback => the disk-full condition was still unresolved at the end of data.

The 'extend' failures are all on the same single relation base/16402/2619, and that relation is still failing 1h44m after the 15:12Z rollback: 139 ERRORs, one pattern 'could not extend file "base/<n>/<n>": No space left on device', first 'base/16402/2619' at 2026-06-01T15:01:39Z, last_match 2026-06-01T16:56:40Z. The blocked relation does not change and the error never stops.

findings.statement: ledger-db connections_active shows no collapse or step in the post-rollback window: it stays flat ~61-64 avg (min 54.84, max 68.34, mean 62.15) across every 8-minute bucket from 13:00Z through 16:52Z, i.e. a subset of writers keeps holding connections after 15:12Z rather than the datastore being drained or restarted.

No ledger-db log line in 14:30-16:59Z contains the string 'portfolio', and no ledger-db log at ERROR level contains it either in 13:00-16:59Z; the log query for 'portfolio' returned total_matched 0 with truncated=false (data_range 11:00Z-16:59Z). So ledger-db logs do NOT name portfolio-service, and the 2619 relation's owning table cannot be attributed from the available logs.

ledger-db's full metric set offers no per-client/write-scoped counters at all: available_metrics are exactly ['connections_active','cpu_pct','disk_used_pct','replication_lag_ms','slow_queries_per_min']. There is therefore no metric on this datastore that could show portfolio-service-specific write/query activity.

Because every one of these 139 extend-failures targets one relation (base/16402/2619) while connections stay flat, the writer that owns the table behind 2619 is the one whose writes are blocked; writers whose tables are already fully allocated (or write already-allocated rows) are not blocked by a full disk and need not show the error. This is the mechanism by which one of the four ledger-db writers (portfolio-service) can remain untouched despite the disk being full.
